newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin warns NATO ahead of Paris accord.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin warns NATO ahead of Paris accord.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin defended an accord he plans to sign with NATO on Tuesday, but warned that any moves by the western alliance to bring in former Soviet republics would "fully undermine" its relations with Moscow.

In an interview with Itar-Tass news agency published by the Kremlin on Monday, Yeltsin said the accord protected Russia's national interests and minimised any damage arising from NATO's plans to invite some former Warsaw Pact countries to join.

"The negative consequences of the expansion of NATO will be reduced to a minimum. This way we will not slip towards confrontation, which would inevitably involve big expenses for arms, a new militarisation of political thinking," he said.

But Yeltsin, who left for Paris later on Monday to sign a Founding Act between Moscow and the Western defence alliance, also reiterated Moscow's general opposition to NATO's plans to invite new members.
"It is fraught with the risk of destabilising Europe," the president said.
The alliance is expected to issue the first invitations to prospective new members -- expected to be Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- at a summit in the Spanish capital Madrid in July.
Yeltsin declined to say whether or not he planned to attend the summit, saying he would have to see how future consultations with the alliance progressed.

Moscow is most concerned by the desire of some former Soviet republics, primarily the Baltic states Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia, to join the alliance and is angered by NATO's refusal to rule out future membership for them.
"I hope that through an open dialogue we will be able to convince those and other countries that their security will not increase by bringing them closer to NATO," Yeltsin said.
"I do not even allow a thought that such a dialogue would fail. This would fully undermine relations between Russia and NATO."
Yeltsin's spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said this would force Russia to review strategy and seek alliances in the east.

"We have proved that we have reliable partners in Asia, but that would not be our choice," he told a Paris news conference. Russia and China last month signed a treaty cutting troops on their common border and hailed a new era of partnership.
Yeltsin said the accord contained binding guarantees that NATO would not post nuclear weapons or build up its forces on the territory of the new members it takes in from the former Soviet bloc.
"We managed to secure in the document an obligation, I stress obligation, that such weapons would not be posted there and there would be no preparations to do so," he said.
"There is firm understanding that there will be no build-up of the forces of the alliance or any additional permanent stationing of NATO forces near our borders," Yeltsin said.
He said the deal created a mechanism for consultations and cooperation. "It allows, on an equal basis, joint consideration and resolution of the questions of security in Europe."

While it addresses some of Russia's concerns over the Western defence alliance's eastward expansion, the Act does not prevent the enlargement which Yeltsin once said could ignite the "flame of war" across Europe.
NATO stopped short of promising Russia not to move military forces onto the territory of new members and said Moscow would not have a veto over alliance decision-making.
In a sign the accord would not end Russia's efforts to limit NATO expansion, Yeltsin held out hope for a future change in Europe's security architecture.

"The alternative is in creating a general and sweeping security system for the whole of Europe which will take into consideration security interests of every state, irrespective of its size, geographic position, economic or military potential."
